newsitem.title: UK: Almost too late for test-tube baby after 35 - study.
newsitem.headline: Almost too late for test-tube baby after 35 - study.

text.p: A woman's chances of giving birth to a test-tube baby plummet sharply after the age of 35, British doctors reported on Friday. Allan Templeton and colleagues at the University of Aberdeen found that 45-year-old women had only a two percent chance of giving birth each time they were treated. Those over 45 have no chance, they wrote in a report in the Lancet medical journal.
Templeton analysed clinical records involving nearly 37,000 cycles of IVF. Each couple typically has several treatments.
For IVF, doctors usually treat a woman with drugs to get her to ovulate. They remove the eggs with a needle and put them in a laboratory dish with sperm from her husband, partner or a donor.
Fertilised eggs are put back into the woman's womb.
Doctors know the rate of success is fairly low and say women often undergo six to 10 cycles of this treatment.
Templeton found the overall success rate was 14 percent per treatment. Women aged 25 to 30 were most likely to conceive this way and have a 16 to 17 percent chance of having a baby.
But the rate dropped sharply, with 35-year-olds at 14 percent, 40-year-olds only having a seven percent chance of success and 45-year-olds looking at a two percent chance.
"No pregnancies were recorded in women older than 45 years," they wrote in their report in the Lancet medical journal.
They found that women over the age of 29 could increase their chances by using a donated egg and women who had been pregnant before had a better chance, too.
And if IVF was going to work, it would probably work sooner rather than later. The more often IVF failed, the less chance there was of success with another treatment.
British fertility experts said the figures were not surprising.
"It's true of course that as women age, it gets worse," said Elliot Philipps, who worked with the teams that pioneered IVF in the 1970s.
Philipps said that over a series of cycles, a woman's chances of a successful pregnancy went up to 60 to 70 percent.
"The new IVF techniques do increase the chances," he added. These would include ICSI, when a sperm is helped along in its work by being injected into the egg.
Lord Robert Winston of London's Hammersmith Hospital said success rates varied greatly from clinic to clinic.

"There may be a number of reasons why some clinics get poor results, not least of which is the way they decide which patients to treat," he said. Some clinics would treat only patients with a good chance of success, such as younger women.
The world's first test-tube baby was Louise Brown, born 18 years ago in 1978. Now more than 19,000 couples try IVF every year in Britain, with more than 3,000 babies resulting.
